item.title: Fukuoka Art Museum — Guide
item.description: The Fukuoka Art Museum, set in a corner of Ohori Park, is one of the leading art museums in Kyushu, reopened after a major renovation with a bright, welcoming design. Its wide-ranging collection spans two main strands: historic Japanese and Asian art, including Buddhist sculpture, tea-ceremony ceramics and old works connected to the region, and modern and contemporary art, with pieces by international masters such as Dalí, Miró, Chagall and Andy Warhol alongside Japanese artists.

item.title: Moerenuma Park — Guide
item.description: Moerenuma Park, on the northeastern edge of Sapporo, is a remarkable green space conceived as a single, unified work of art by the renowned Japanese-American sculptor Isamu Noguchi. Built on the site of a former waste treatment plant and completed in 2005 (following Noguchi’s master plan), the entire park is essentially one vast sculpture, blending art, architecture and nature across roughly 190 hectares. Its striking features include Mount Moere, a perfectly geometric man-made hill offering panoramic views; the Glass Pyramid ‘HIDAMARI’, a gleaming structure housing galleries, a shop and café; the elegant Sea Fountain, which performs choreographed water shows; a beach-like play area, and geometric play equipment.

item.title: Otsuka Museum of Art: Masterpieces in Ceramic — Guide
item.description: The Otsuka Museum of Art in Naruto is one of Japan’s most unusual and impressive museums: an enormous gallery displaying over a thousand of the West’s greatest artworks, all as full-size ceramic reproductions. Using a special technique, masterpieces from more than 190 galleries worldwide — the Mona Lisa, Van Gogh’s sunflowers, Monet’s water lilies, Vermeer, Munch’s Scream and countless more — are reproduced onto ceramic boards at exact original scale, faithful in colour and detail and, remarkably, near-permanent.

item.title: Roppongi Hills & Tokyo City View — Guide
item.description: Roppongi Hills is a large, modern urban development in the Roppongi district, centred on the 54-storey Mori Tower and a hub of shopping, dining, art and nightlife. Its main draw for visitors is the Tokyo City View observation deck near the top of the tower, which offers spectacular 360-degree panoramas over the city — with a superb view of Tokyo Tower lit up at night as its centrepiece, plus the Skytree, Tokyo Bay and, on clear days, Mount Fuji.

item.title: Saga Prefectural Museum and Art Museum — Guide
item.description: The Saga Prefectural Museum and the adjoining Saga Prefectural Art Museum, set together beside the greenery of Saga Castle park in the heart of the city, form the prefecture’s main cultural complex. The museum covers Saga’s natural history, archaeology and history — including material connected to the Yoshinogari ancient site, the prefecture’s important role in Japan’s modernisation, and its ceramics and culture — through well-presented exhibits. The art museum next door displays works by artists connected to Saga alongside changing exhibitions.

item.title: Tokyo National Museum — Guide
item.description: The Tokyo National Museum (Tokyo Kokuritsu Hakubutsukan), founded in 1872 and set in Ueno Park, is Japan’s oldest and largest museum, and home to the world’s most comprehensive collection of Japanese art and archaeology. Its vast holdings — over 110,000 items including scores of designated National Treasures and Important Cultural Properties — span the whole sweep of Japanese culture: samurai swords and armour, exquisite Buddhist sculpture, painted screens and scrolls, ceramics, lacquerware, ukiyo-e woodblock prints, kimono and textiles, and archaeological finds.

item.title: Tottori Sand Museum: Sculptures Carved from Sand — Guide
item.description: The Sand Museum, right beside the Tottori Sand Dunes, is the only museum in the world devoted to sculpture made from sand. Each year it invites top sand sculptors from around the globe to carve enormous, astonishingly detailed works — figures, buildings and scenes several metres tall — around a single theme, such as a different country or civilisation. The results, held together only by water and packing, are displayed for about a year before being returned to loose sand and rebuilt anew for the next theme.

item.title: Akita Museum of Art: Foujita's Mural & Tadao Ando — Guide
item.description: The Akita Museum of Art, designed by Tadao Ando, is home to Tsuguharu Foujita’s monumental mural ‘Events in Akita’ — one of the largest canvases in Japan, depicting the prefecture’s festivals and daily life. Ando’s spiral staircase and a rooftop triangular water pool that frames Senshu Park make the building itself a work of art. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Akita City, Akita Hours ~10:00–18:00 (closed irregular) Admission Around ¥310 (collection) Time needed About 1 hour Best time Year-round What to See Foujita’s vast mural ‘Events in Akita’.

item.title: Hakone Open-Air Museum Guide: Tickets, Art & Access
item.description: The Hakone Open-Air Museum was Japan’s first open-air sculpture park, and it remains one of the most delightful art experiences near Tokyo. Set across a sweeping hillside in the Hakone mountains, it scatters more than 100 sculptures by masters like Henry Moore and Niki de Saint Phalle across lawns, gardens and valley views. Highlights include a dedicated Picasso Pavilion, the stained-glass tower Symphonic Sculpture you can climb, playful works kids can clamber on, and a free hot-spring foot bath to soak tired feet.

item.title: Naoshima Art Island, Kagawa: The Complete Visitor's Guide
item.description: Naoshima is a small island of roughly 8 square kilometres in the Seto Inland Sea, about 50 minutes by ferry from Takamatsu. In the early 1990s, it was a quiet island with an ageing fishing population, a modest industrial presence, and no particular reason to appear on any travel itinerary. Over the following three decades, the Fukutake Foundation — the philanthropic arm of Benesse Holdings, based in Okayama — transformed it into one of the world’s most celebrated destinations for contemporary art and architecture.

item.title: Hakone Complete Guide: Onsen, Art Museums & Mt. Fuji Views
item.description: Hakone is Japan’s most visited onsen resort for good reason: within 90 minutes of Shinjuku, a completely different world opens up. Active volcanoes, a mountain lake reflecting Mt. Fuji, outdoor sculpture gardens, and hundreds of ryokan offering hot spring baths with mountain views. The challenge isn’t finding things to do — it’s choosing between them. This guide breaks down every decision you’ll need to make. Choosing Your Base: The 17 Onsen Areas Hakone comprises 17 separate onsen resort areas (温泉地), each with a distinct character and elevation.
